rules.rule_en: The subject usually comes before the verb (e.g., The dog bit the horse).
The object usually comes after the verb (e.g., The horse bit the dog).
When there is an indirect object and a direct object, the indirect precedes the direct (e.g., Lend me your ears).
When the adjective is used attributively it comes before the noun which it qualifies (e.g., Few cats like cold water).
When the adjective is used predicatively it comes after the noun (e.g., The child is asleep).
The adjective phrase comes immediately after the noun (e.g., The tops of the mountains were covered with snow).
The adverb is generally placed close to the word which it modifies (e.g., Nothing ever happens by chance).
When an adverb is intended to modify the sentence as a whole, it is placed at the beginning of a sentence (e.g., Certainly he made a fool of himself).
All qualifying clauses are placed as close as possible to the words which they qualify (e.g., He died in the village where he was born).

examples.prompt_en: Jane Eyre is an orphan. She lives with her aunt Mrs. Reed. Mrs. Reed does not like Jane because Jane is not her daughter. Jane’s uncle Mr. Reed likes Jane, but he dies. He makes Mrs. Reed promise to take care of Jane, but instead she sends Jane away. Jane is ten years old, she is sent to Lowood school. Jane graduates and stays there to teach. She leaves for Thornfield, where she is a governess. She is very happy there.
examples.answer_en: Jane Eyre is an orphan who lives with her aunt Mrs. Reed. Although Mrs. Reed does not like Jane because she is not her daughter, Jane’s uncle Mr. Reed likes Jane. He makes Mrs. Reed promise to take care of Jane before he dies, but instead, she sends Jane away. When Jane is ten years old, she is sent to Lowood school. Later, Jane graduates and stays there to teach, then leaves for Thornfield to work as a governess where she is very happy.
